problems.description: test_notification_server.py defines classes not using PascalCase and module-level constants not UPPER_CASE (the 2 SonarQube convention violations, 0.91 score).

Commit wholesale-replaced the existing Flask seed (models/routes/error-handling seams, ~110 lines removed) with a different-domain WebSocket server rather than building on or preserving the existing structure; no existing patterns were reused.

Cognitive complexity rose +9 — proportionate to growing a single-file stub into a real async server (broadcast fan-out + lifecycle logic), but the class has grown responsibilities (registry, routing, health, lifecycle).

strengths: Zero new bugs, -2 smells, 0.0% duplication per SonarQube; net +256 lines is a complete, functional replacement app rather than scaffolding
Clean single-file layout with PascalCase server class, snake_case helpers, full type hints and __future__ annotations
Thread-safe client registry guarded by a lock shared across the async loop and HTTP thread
Proper async lifecycle with graceful start/stop (server close, connection drain, health thread shutdown)
commit_reviews.summary: A well-constructed, low-debt greenfield rewrite (bugs 0, smells -2, conventions 0.91) that scores high on code quality but low on continuity — it discards the existing Flask architecture entirely rather than respecting prior seams, which is defensible only because this is an intentional session-1 greenfield commit.

problems.description: Channel cleanup logic is duplicated between the disconnect path and the unsubscribe handler (discard subscriber, drop empty channel), which the +10.3% duplication and +8 smells measurements reflect; extract a shared helper.
Cognitive complexity +59 in _handle_message from nested channel-routing branches; routing decision could be factored into per-message-type handlers.
A 'direct' message carrying a 'channel' field silently drops when the sender is not subscribed to it; silent failure makes misrouting hard to debug.

strengths: Faithfully implements the Session 2 spec: subscribe/unsubscribe types, channel-scoped routing, and both REST endpoints (GET /channels, GET /channels/{name}/subscribers).
Respects existing patterns: registry_lock discipline, JSON body with 404 handling in _HealthHandler, list-comprehension over clients under lock — no new dependencies.
Input sanitization is correct: urllib.parse unquote + rejecting channel names containing '/' prevents path confusion.
commit_reviews.summary: Correct, pattern-respecting feature addition that matches the story spec exactly, but its +8 smells and +10.3% duplicated channel-cleanup logic tip the net impact to neutral rather than better.

problems.description: MessageStore uses blocking sqlite3 calls (connect/execute/commit) under a threading.Lock; when add() is invoked from the async WebSocket path this blocks the event loop for all clients instead of offloading to an executor or using aiosqlite.
Bare `except Exception` around Redis setup in start() silently disables cross-instance message distribution with no logging or status surfaced, making multi-instance failure invisible at runtime.

`Redis = Any` fallback when redis is not importable yields an untyped client; the graceful-degradation seam is reasonable but any call on the fallback is unchecked and could fail at runtime instead of import time.
Two measured convention violations in test_notification_server.py: test class names should be PascalCase and module-level constants should be UPPER_CASE.

strengths: Graceful single-instance degradation when Redis is unavailable keeps the existing server fully functional
MessageStore encapsulates persistence cleanly with a documented open/close lifecycle and thread-safe access consistent with the existing registry_lock pattern
New /messages endpoint follows the established HTTP route-dispatch pattern and clamps pagination (limit 0-1000) with input validation
Python 3.10+ union syntax and `from __future__ import annotations` kept consistent with the existing code style
commit_reviews.summary: A solid integration commit that adds Redis fan-out and SQLite persistence to the notification service while following existing route and locking patterns, though the blocking sqlite I/O on the async loop and the silent Redis failure handling introduce technical debt.

problems.description: BaseTransport.start() raises NotImplementedError but stop() silently no-ops; inconsistent abstract contract — the base class should either be fully abstract or define a symmetric default for stop() that signals 'not supported'.
BaseTransport.__init__ uses a forward-ref string annotation ("NotificationServer") that could be avoided with a TYPE_CHECKING import plus deferred annotation evaluation.

The two reported convention violations (PascalCase class, UPPER_CASE module constant) live in test_notification_server.py, which this commit does not touch — they are pre-existing, not introduced by the agent.

strengths: Extracts a clean strategy seam (BaseTransport ABC + WebSocketTransport) so NotificationServer is transport-agnostic; concrete server internals no longer leak into the orchestrator.
Mechanically improves the codebase: -35 cognitive complexity and -2 code smells with no new bugs or duplication per SonarQube.
Follows existing style: snake_case methods, type hints on public signatures, consistent Any-typed injection for external deps (redis_client, transport).
commit_reviews.summary: A well-scoped transport abstraction refactor that improves encapsulation and reduces complexity substantially, though note the reported convention violations predate this commit in an untouched test file.

problems.description: Cognitive complexity +35 from the message-routing branch in _handle_message and the new /history handler; the added branching in a single dispatch method is becoming hard to follow.

RATE_LIMIT=0 is treated as deny-all (return False) rather than unlimited, which is surprising given the env default of 100 and max(0, ...) clamping; an explicit sentinel or clearer semantics would avoid a misconfiguration footgun.
test_notification_server.py violates two conventions: a class not using PascalCase and a module-level constant not UPPER_CASE (matches the 0.91 convention score, 2 violations).
New features (history endpoint, TTL cleanup loop) have no coverage shown in the diff — only rate limiting gets a test, leaving the cleanup task and /history pagination untested.

strengths: Extracts shared _query helper, de-duplicating list() and history() rather than copy-pasting the SQL row-mapping logic.
Follows the established asyncio task lifecycle — _cleanup_task created in start() and cancelled in stop(), mirroring _subscriber_task.
Rate limiting reuses the existing Redis path with a local fallback, consistent with the project's dual-backend pattern.
The /history handler mirrors the existing route structure and validates the since ISO timestamp before querying.
commit_reviews.summary: A well-structured cross-cutting commit that refactors shared query logic, adds history/rate-limit/TTL features consistent with existing patterns, and slightly reduces smells (smells -2) at the cost of raised cognitive complexity and minor test conventions.

compounding_issues: S1's decision to embed both WebSocket and HTTP serving in a single NotificationServer class made notification_server.py grow to 442 lines by S5; the S4 transport refactor extracted only the WebSocket listener, leaving HTTP, SQLite, Redis, and rate limiting in the monolith

The transport abstraction introduced in S4 is effectively unimplemented beyond WebSocket — _create_transport raises for any non-websocket value, so the 'pluggable transport' promise is structural only
S1's threading.RLock guard over asyncio-managed client dicts persisted through every session, mixing threading and asyncio primitives in an event-loop-only codebase
S3's Redis integration degrades silently (falls back to in-memory/single-instance on any ping failure), which can mask deployment misconfigurations
The S1 seed's app.py was almost entirely discarded in Session 1's greenfield rewrite, wasting the seed scaffolding
key_decisions: S1 discarded the seed implementation in favor of a clean monolithic async server owning both WebSocket and HTTP in one class
S2 extended the wire protocol with channel subscribe/unsubscribe, adding a channel registry kept in sync across subscribe, disconnect, and cleanup paths
S3 added Redis pub/sub fan-out and SQLite message persistence (with graceful degradation when Redis is absent), making the server multi-instance capable
S4 extracted a BaseTransport/WebSocketTransport abstraction so the server routes messages through a pluggable transport layer
S5 added per-client rate limiting (Redis-backed with local fallback), a message TTL retention policy with a background cleanup loop, and a /history HTTP endpoint
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved steadily across all five sessions. The story moves logically from a greenfield monolithic core (S1), through a protocol-level feature (channels, S2) and integration (Redis pub/sub + SQLite persistence, S3), to an architectural refactor extracting a transport abstraction (S4), and finally cross-cutting concerns (rate limiting, retention TTL, history endpoint, S5). Test coverage grew in lockstep with implementation size (4 → 10 tests, 154 → 442 server lines), and the final commit passes 15 tests with 1 skip. The progression is natural and cumulative, with each session building on the prior protocol and storage decisions rather than reworking them, though the S4 refactor was partial and did not prevent continued monolith growth.
story_review.summary: A highly coherent five-session arc that progressed naturally from greenfield core to channels, Redis/SQLite integration, a transport abstraction, and finally cross-cutting operational concerns, with quality and test coverage improving monotonically throughout.
